correctness.rationale: For n>=2 and ordinary multiplicity S(n)=sum p nu_p(n), the four possibilities prime/prime, prime/semiprime, semiprime/prime and semiprime/semiprime exhaust Omega(n),Omega(n+1)<=2. Adjacent primes 2,3 have unequal S. In prime/semiprime case p=ab-1=a+b gives (a-1)(b-1)=2 and uniquely a,b=2,3 so n=5. In reverse case a+b=ab+1 forces (a-1)(b-1)=0, impossible for primes. Two semiprimes ab,cd with cd-ab=1 and c+d=a+b yield the exact factorization 1=(c-a)(b-c). The two sign choices force three consecutive integers to be prime, necessarily 2,3,4, impossible. Repetition a=b and c=d is included; independent direct factorization scan through n=20000 found only n=5. Universal proof is symbolic, not finite.

evidence: The published prime-containing theorem establishes 5,6 whenever one entry is prime, with no restriction on the other. The other result concerns sigma(n)=sigma(n+1), not S(n)=S(n+1).
broader_coverage.reasoning: The stronger prime-containing theorem covers all low-Omega patterns involving a prime, but not two semiprimes. Equality of divisor sums sigma is logically different from equality of prime-factor sums S.

value.rationale: This is the complete first nontrivial factor-complexity boundary for the classical Ruth–Aaron invariant when multiplicities count. It closes an ordinary natural prime/semiprime comparison, explicitly including squares, by a sharp obstruction to two neighboring semiprimes. It is elementary and narrow, but a genuine natural exact classification rather than a generic rephrasing or an arbitrary numerical slice; no claims beyond Omega<=2 are made.
